messages:
maya: Ran a focused cutover sweep this morning comparing streaming (SSE) vs non-stream (HTTP chunked/WebSocket) endpoints across GPU families and regions. Putting highlights and a tiny data dump below — TL;DR at the top. :chart_with_upwards_trend:

sam: nice, TL;DR please :)

maya: TL;DR — For 128-token avg prompts: SSE gives higher steady throughput but has a wider p99 on g5 nodes in us-west. On h100 the throughput gain narrows and p99 is comparable. Kernel selection (tf32 vs int8 paths) matters more for non-stream endpoints under batchy workloads.

kai: can you share the exact loadgen incantation and the key numbers?

maya: ```
# loadgen prototype we used
./bench/loadgen --model llama-2-13b --mode sse --url https://api.redwood/test-sse --concurrency 16 --seq 128 --duration 300 --workers 8 --region us-west-2
./bench/loadgen --model llama-2-13b --mode http --url https://api.redwood/test-http --concurrency 16 --seq 128 --duration 300 --workers 8 --region us-west-2
```

toni: did you control for cache warm/cold?

maya: yes — each run had two phases: cold (first 120s) and warm (last 180s). Below are aggregated warm-phase numbers (steady-state).

jen: curious about GPU family split. numbers?

maya: small paste of warm-phase numbers (throughput = requests/sec, p50/p99 latency in ms). These are per-endpoint steady-state averages across 3 runs:```
endpoint,gpu,region,throughput,p50,p99
sse,g5,us-west-2,320,28,210
http,g5,us-west-2,200,35,140
sse,h100,us-west-2,450,22,170
http,h100,us-west-2,380,25,160
sse,g5,us-east-1,340,26,190
http,g5,us-east-1,210,33,130
```

sam: interesting that SSE p99 on g5/us-west is 210ms while http p99 is 140ms despite SSE having higher throughput. any idea why?

maya: hypothesis — SSE's smaller per-chunk network overhead increases connection pressure on our edge load balancers in us-west cluster (higher concurrent long-lived connections), which amplifies tail latency under contended NIC / proxy threads. On h100 the model runtime dominates which mutes the networking tail.

kai: kernel/quantization notes?

maya: we ran two kernel paths: default tf32 (no quant) and int8-quantized kernels. For non-stream endpoints we could batch more aggressively, so int8 gave ~1.8x throughput on g5 but quality regressions were visible on long-context prompts. SSE couldn't batch across requests as effectively so int8 gains were ~1.25x there.

toni: So what's your recommendation for a rollout policy for product teams that care about p99 <200ms?

maya: recommendation:
- prefer non-stream (http/ws) for strict p99 SLOs in g5 regions; it gets you tighter tail at moderate throughput.
- use SSE for latency-sensitive p50 and higher throughput on h100 or when you have aggressive connection stack tuning in the edge.
- enable KV-cache warmup and prefetch to shrink SSE tail by ~10-15%.
- for cutover: canary 5% traffic shift to SSE in a region with metrics gating (p50, p95, p99, error rate, CPU/NIC queue depth).

jen: any short config snippets for the edge tuning you mentioned?

maya: small notes we've been testing: ```
# nginx/proxy: increase keepalive_requests and worker_connections, tune accept_mutex off for pinned CPUs
keepalive_timeout 60s;
worker_connections 4096;
worker_cpu_affinity 0 1 2 3;
```
Also procmgr: pin proxy threads away from runtime GPU-serving cores; avoid socket stealing during bursts.

bench-bot: test-run summary uploaded: https://internal.redwood/bench/2148501234 (csv + charts).

sam: next steps? more regions or more models?

maya: follow-ups: run same sweep on a longer seq (512) and include cold-start tail breakdown per region. Also test with real user prompt mix (not uniform seq=128) before recommending default endpoint. I'll open a short PR to add the loadgen scripts and CSV to the repo.

kai: thanks — can you drop the PR link here when ready?

maya: will do. :thumbsup:
